extracted.intended_audience: academic economists and empirical researchers in labor economics/econometrics
extracted.subtask_description: Estimating how much of labor earnings variability is forecastable (known to agents at decision time) versus unforecastable (uncertainty) using schooling choice data, earnings histories, and factor-structure econometric methods. The paper applies and extends the Cunha–Heckman–Navarro (CHN) framework to NLS cohorts, performs identification/estimation, and quantifies contributions to inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish predictable vs unpredictable components of earnings
rubrics_metrics.description: A large empirical literature documents variability in wages; variability is not the same as uncertainty. Some variability may be due to components predictable by agents (forecastable) and some to components unpredictable at the time decisions are made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Join choice data with earnings data to estimate the fraction of future earnings that is forecastable versus unforecastable; recognize that statistical decompositions (permanent/transitory) do not necessarily map to forecastable vs unforecastable components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply CHN methodology to identify forecastable fraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the methodology of Cunha, Heckman and Navarro (2005) to join choice data with earnings data to estimate the fraction of future earnings that is forecastable and how it changed over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the CHN framework (factor models, choice/earnings joint estimation) and web supplement identification results; test which factors enter the decision index I to determine what agents know when choosing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forecastability test via choice correlation (V = PV − E(PV|I))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the information set is properly specified, the residual corresponding to the component of PV that is not forecastable in the first period, V = PV − E(PV | I), should not predict the decision D1. E(PV | I) is predictable; V measures uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize by constructing PV ex post and checking whether its unpredictable residual correlates with observed choices (S). Related to Sims (1972) noncausality test but measures fraction of future Yt that predict current D1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnings equation specification and error-mean assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Earnings for schooling state s are modeled as Ys,t = Xβs,t + Us,t (s = 0,1, t = 1,...,T) with finite means and error term satisfying E(Us,t | X) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linearity is used for familiarity and simplicity though analysis does not require linearity; include age-specific returns to capture post-school investment effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schooling choice modeled as expected present-value maximization under risk neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents are assumed risk neutral and choose schooling based on maximizing expected present value income given their information set I: S = 1[I ≥ 0], where I = E(PV | I) minus costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify costs C = Zγ + UC and define µI and UI accordingly; be explicit about what elements of X, Z, βs,t, εC are assumed in the agent's information set when testing forecastability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use test scores as noisy measures of latent cognitive ability (factor θ1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test scores Mk are modeled as Mk = X^M β^M_k + θ1 α^M_k + ε^M_k, where θ1 is a common factor (latent ability) and test scores are noisy measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test score data facilitate identification but are not essential; normalize a factor loading (e.g. α^M_1 = 1) to set scale of θ1; when test-score availability is limited, supplement with proxies (e.g. 'Knowledge of the World of Work').

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose earnings errors using factor-structure approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose disturbance terms in earnings into common factors and idiosyncratic errors: Us,t = θ α0_s,t + εs,t, enabling partitioning of realized earnings into orthogonal components some of which may be forecastable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor models are conceptually convenient and can approximate general error processes; choose number of factors to fit data (authors use three factors empirically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify which factors are in agents' information set via covariance with choice index
rubrics_metrics.description: From the correlation between S and realized incomes, one can identify the covariance between choice index I and Ys,t; if αk,I ≠ 0 then factor θk is correlated with I and acted on by agents; if αk,I = 0, it is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discrete choice index identification (observed up to scale) combined with factor analysis and test-score information to determine which factors are forecastable at decision time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address self-selection in earnings observations for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts observe only the earnings stream associated with chosen schooling state s, creating self-selection; CHN provide conditions to identify factor loadings and factor distributions using self-selected samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply CHN identification conditions (detailed in web supplement) and impose necessary normalizations; test-score data help but are not strictly required for identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize factor loadings for identification (scale indeterminacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The identification of the model requires the normalization of some factor loadings because the scale of θ is otherwise indeterminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impose normalization conventions (e.g., set a loading to 1) and report normalizations in appendix; be explicit about which loadings are fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate factor and error distributions via mixtures of normals and MCMC
rubrics_metrics.description: Each factor θk is modeled as a mixture of Jk normal distributions and idiosyncratic errors εs,t are also mixtures; estimation uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose adequate number of mixture components (authors found Jk = 4 for factors, 3 for εs,t adequate); check that additional components don't improve fit; report prior choices and convergence diagnostics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model earnings in levels (not logs) under risk-neutral valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: The dependent variable is earnings (levels) rather than log earnings because under risk neutrality agents act on expected earnings and we fit a nonparametric error distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify level specification by decision-theoretic argument; note conventional log specification is for goodness-of-fit but may not align with decision model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess model fit by comparing predicted and observed density functions and formal tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare actual and predicted densities of earnings (e.g., kernel density estimates) across ages and schooling groups and perform formal goodness-of-fit tests of equality of densities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present density plots (overall and by subgroup), conduct formal tests within schooling groups for most ages, and show supplementary fit diagnostics in appendices or web supplements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for truncation of observed earnings in present-value and cost measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Because earnings data are observed only up to mid-30s (age T*), truncated discounted earnings after observation are absorbed into the estimated cost C; estimated cost therefore includes expected returns realized after T*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state truncation horizon T* and interpret estimated costs accordingly; consider sensitivity to choice of discount rate and truncation period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize age-period-cohort (APC) identification limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is the standard lack of simultaneous identification of age, period and cohort effects, so cohort effects cannot be separately identified in the presence of age and time effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge APC limitation, interpret time-dummies estimates as potentially absorbing cohort effects, and cite literature (Heckman & Robb 1985) for discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model macro uncertainty with time dummies and test forecastability
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture macro uncertainty by introducing time dummies into the earnings equations; tests indicate these time dummies do not enter the schooling choice equation (i.e., macro shocks are unforecastable by agents at decision time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate share of total unforecastable variance due to macro shocks and report trends (authors find macro uncertainty decreased and is a small fraction of total uncertainty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose total variance into forecastable (heterogeneity) and unforecastable (uncertainty) components and quantify contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute total variance of present value of earnings and the portion due to unforecastable components Var(Ps) to determine how much of observed increases in inequality are attributable to uncertainty vs predictable heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report cohort comparisons (e.g., percent increases by schooling group), tabulate results (Table 3), and express contributions as percentages of total variance growth (e.g., 60% of increase in high-school earnings variability due to uncertainty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze age profiles of forecastable and unforecastable variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot variances of forecastable and unforecastable components by age to show how increases in uncertainty vary across ages (e.g., flat until ~27/28 then increase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these age profiles to interpret when uncertainty accumulates and how divergence across cohorts emerges by age groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulate counterfactuals (shutting down idiosyncratic uncertainty) to assess inequality impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct counterfactual distributions by shutting down idiosyncratic uncertainty (retain heterogeneity only) and compute inequality indices (Gini, Theil, Atkinson) to quantify the role of uncertainty in observed inequality growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep schooling choices fixed to factual economy for some counterfactuals; report percentage changes in inequality indices across cohorts and scenarios (factual vs heterogeneity-only).

rubrics_metrics.name: State and examine preference assumptions (risk neutrality vs risk aversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The baseline analysis assumes risk neutrality (and/or full insurance); the authors note modeling risk aversion explicitly would raise more general identification questions and reference related work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss robustness by citing models with risk aversion and market structure (e.g., Navarro 2007) or by sensitivity analyses; be explicit about how preference assumptions affect interpretation of choices and valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternative proxies when test-score data are limited
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple test scores per respondent are unavailable (NLS/1966), supplement with proxies for cognitive achievement such as 'Knowledge of the World of Work' tests (occupation knowledge, education associated with occupation, earnings comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for parental education, siblings, urban residence, birth year dummies when using proxies; demonstrate correlations between proxies and formal test scores to justify use.
